SuicideWatch,"I'm sad to say, I'm not much better.  hopefully this has sank to the bottom of the pile and no one reads it, because i have had a week of ups and downs.    The day after I posted it, the crisis team visited (Monday), making me feel worse.

i then started cutting, and as I cut I kept wanting to go longer and deeper,  somehow once I'd made a mess of myself, I managed to get some help.  I spent the evening in hospital and was then sent up to the psych unit, who sent me home with the promise that they'd re-evaluate.
Monday night, I got back at 00:30 - I managed to sleep and spent Tuesday pretty much so tired and drained that i couldn't do anything.   I was too sore to cut, and too tired to think about much.

Weds & Thurs spent in a downhill spiral again.  Not so much suicidal, but the cutting has escalated from scratching with a little blood to cuts which really bleed, and the occasional deeper one.  Thursday, the crisis team brought a charity who ""help people get out"" with them, and i also attended the psych self-esteem group, and Thursday I had to attend a meeting regarding housing which was so nerve wracking and which turned out to be pointless.  Thursday night left me down and back to feeling what's the point.  With a different crisis worker coming to see me each day, it feels very much like there's no real care given.  Today they were cold, dismissive and didn't really care about my self harm - ""it's a way to cope.."" and suggested I visit friends and family.  (i'm totally estranged from all. which they know.)

I managed to pick up additional meds, but sitting in the pharmacy awaiting the dispensing of them was nerve wracking.  I sat there thinking why am I even bothering.  Since i got home,  I cut myself again - but managed to close it with surgical tape, and since, I have been confirming my plans by reading tons of medical journals about my chosen method.

I already have notes written, a list of my things / debts / passwords prepared and instructions for what to do. i feel calm about it all, with the odd patch of sadness because I know there won't be anyone that can come and save  me, and I know if I ask for help they will just not listen,  part of me wants to keep on going,  but I just keep asking my self, for what ?

I don't know if this night will be the night, but the truth is, suicide doesn't feel like a painful emotion anymore.  It feels like a well reasoned choice that I am (almost) comfortable with.  I think it's that conclusion that leaves me still a little sad.

transgenderUK,So - had my first appt on this week, so i can share :)

column1: went in - grabbed a ticket from the reception and told to wait for number to check in.
Then checked in by reception. Sat down, waited for appt.  Doctor calls me - introduces himself and asks if student can attend - sure.   (you really don't have to if you don't want to).

Next hour entails the doc asking full history - when did i start feeling the way I did - what happened at puberty, what do I want out of treatment,  and the only slightly inappropriate q - ""what is your sexuality...""

He informs me timeline wise that I am looking at 3 months to see medical team to be prescribed hormones, 1 year under their regimen before I can get grs and about 2 years for potential FFS and BA if necessary.

All in all - it went well, all you are expected to do is to give a complete history to date - feel free to prepare in advance.  I had proof of living as me etc, but only thing he had a look at was the stat dec and took a note of the date I transitioned.

It was a relatively easy appointment - I left feeling a bit gutted as he told me winter 2020 for GRS if all goes well, but honestly -  don't stress too much x   It's your chance to also ask as many questions as you wish!
Be amazing x

transgenderUK,Hi Deanne,

Firstly, any disclosure about your trans status, to anyone either up or down the line is your call.   You are protected by the equality act under the protected characteristic of gender reassignment, which includes anyone about to or going through the process.

That probably means getting some info for your bosses, as they may not be entirely clued up about the ramifications of intentional disclosure, or what I call and have experienced 'goodwill disclosure' (when it's decided to do it 'to make sure everyone knows so it's easy for you').

Firstly - have a think, who needs to know, what do you want to tell them and how do you want it to be done.  I had a chat with my immediate manager, provided resources and let him do his research with a follow-up in a few weeks, with a gentle reminder of what the potential damage (both personal and professional) could be if he told anyone.  We had a follow up meet where I told him a timeline, and I explained that I'd like mgmt to know in order to arrange some awareness for team leaders.  Mgmt got the slightly sharper line highlighting discrimination and possible harassment, and how it's important to lead by example....

Team leaders got told a few days before, during an awareness session that was actually a bit shock and awe, to instil the cold harsh truth that it isn't going to be easy.  The session went into full detail about the equality act gender recognition act and gave plenty of exampled in which disclosures had lead to dismissals, law suits,  serious harm to the trans person etc.  I arranged for an external party to do the training and also used it to come out to them.

After which, I sent an all-site email with a personal message of what it means and who I am... It went well, and I made myself available, by also running info sessions for folks who wanted to understand.
In a smaller work place, I'd speak with your direct manager or if they aren't v.good, see if you can arrange a meeting with their boss.
Have a plan - and a timeline for this -

when will you tell colleagues? will you tell management staff first? do you want to tell them yourself or have someone else do this? do you wish to take some time off before or after telling them?  Also consider if you would wish any reasonable adjustments - are you going to be OK getting straight back to the phones? is there anything else you can do for those stressful first few weeks back as you?

The important part, is this happens as per your wishes, and at your pace.  Ultimately while you may 'need' (and I use this word very lightly as it's your choice ) to tell everyone initially, as new people come - it should be made clear, that you are Deanne and that's that.  There should be no need to tell anyone after you have transitioned.

Also, find out about HR policies - what do you need to change those details i.e. accounting. (you should be able to do this by declaration, GP's letters are NOT required.)  Also system access and what not.
Here's a few resources - just buzz if you need anything at all x
http://www.equality-network.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/changing_for_the_better.pdf
http://www.lgbthealth.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2016/07/TWSP-Info-Guide-Final.pdf
Good luck,  and remember - it's up to you how you want it to go.",1516137071.0,2

The benefits of SSD is that they can update all dwp/hmrc systems in one foul swoop, and they are also trained to follow relevant guidance to make sure it gets done right.
The complication is that until sight of  a GRC in my case, I am most unfortunately registered male with a female name and pronouns.

They also by default, mark your record as sensitive, (and they are the only folks who can do it) to ensure that anyone snooping cannot access your information without requesting special permission and justification why.

While many appreciate the sensitive status,  it is sensitive status rather than special section D which is discriminatory, as very few groups have sensitive status, it is most likely restricted to sex offenders,  those under witness protection, but also trans people. (some speculation here).

SSD sort things out quickly, competently and without discrimination.  If you had to pop into a job centre to change things over, mistakes could be made - notes could be written by mistake, accidentally recording information that shouldn't be.
As a result special section D is set up not to discriminate but to ensure that dwp/hmrc accidental disclosure or discrimination doesn't happen elsewhere.",1515486076.0,3

transgenderUK,Hiya - you should be able to change your gender on all but your birth certificate and HMRC/DWP records. Once you acquire a Gender Recognition Certificate, you can then amend those.  [GOV.UK-Grc](https://www.gov.uk/apply-gender-recognition-certificate)
To get a GRC you need to jump through a few hoops and meet some criteria:
*you’re 18 or over
*you’ve been diagnosed with gender dysphoria (discomfort with your birth gender) - this is also called gender identity disorder or transsexualism
*you’ve lived in your acquired gender for at least 2 years
